blocks.text: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
heading_path: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

blocks.text: T he Th ird quarterly National Government Budget Implementation Review Report for FY 2024/25 covers 1 July to 31 st March 2025. Th e report has been prepared to comply with Article 228(6) of the Constitution and Section 9 of the Controller of Budget Act, 2016, which requires the Controller of Budget to submit quarterly budget implementation reports for the National and County governments to Parliament.
heading_path: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

blocks.text: Th is is the third budget under the fourth Medium-Term Plan (MTP) (2023-2027) of the Kenya Vision 2030 and is being implemented under the Bottom-up Economic Transformation Agenda (BETA) framework. Under this  framework, the government aims to achieve economic turnaround and inclusive growth by increasing investments in at least five sectors that significantly impact the economy and household welfare. Th ese sectors include agricultural transformation, micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSME), housing and settlement, healthcare, digital superhighway, and creative industry. Th e agenda also focuses on increasing employment, equitable distribution of income, and social security while expanding the tax revenue base and increasing foreign exchange earnings.
heading_path: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

blocks.text: Th e National Government's original gross budget was Kshs.4.49 trillion, revised to Kshs.4.37 trillion in Supplementary Budget I and Kshs.4.64 trillion in Supplementary Budget II, compared to Kshs.4.34 trillion for FY 2023/24. Th e  revised budget comprises Kshs.616.09 billion for ministerial development expenditure, which was 13 per cent of the revised gross national budget and 26 per cent of the revised gross ministerial budget of Kshs.2.35 trillion. Recurrent allocation comprised ministerial recurrent allocation of Kshs.1.73 trillion (37 per cent of the revised gross national budget) and Consolidated Fund Services (CFS) at Kshs.2.29 trillion (49 per cent of the revised gross national budget).
heading_path: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

blocks.text: During the reporting period, receipts into the Consolidated Fund amounted to Kshs.2.75 trillion, representing 62 per cent of the revised net estimates of Kshs.4.47 trillion, compared to the Kshs.2.7 trillion (63 per cent) received in a similar period in FY 2023/24. Th e total exchequer issues from the Consolidated Fund to MDAs, CFS, and the County Governments amounted to Kshs.2.64 trillion, representing 59 per cent of the revised net estimates of Kshs.4.47 trillion, compared to Kshs.2.7 trillion recorded in a similar period in FY 2023/24. Th e exchequer issues comprised Kshs.170.83 billion (48 per cent) for ministerial development expenditure, Kshs. 991.75 billion (70 per cent) for ministerial recurrent expenditure, Kshs. 1,223.30 billion (53 per cent) to CFS and Kshs. 255.54 billion (61 per cent) to County governments as equitable shareable revenue. County government exchequer issues from the national government included Kshs.30.83 billion for June 2024 arrears.
heading_path: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

blocks.text: Th e national government's total expenditure for the first nine months amounted to Kshs.2.86 trillion, representing 62 per cent of the national government's revised gross estimates of Kshs.4.64 trillion compared to Kshs.2.91 trillion  (64  per  cent)  recorded  in  a  similar  FY  2023/24  period. Th is  expenditure comprised ministerial development expenditure of Kshs.338.18 billion (with an absorption rate of 55 per cent), recurrent ministerial expenditure at Kshs.1.20 trillion (absorption rate of 70 per cent) and CFS expenditure at Kshs.1.31 trillion (an absorption rate of 57 per cent).
heading_path: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

blocks.text: Development expenditure with the highest spending included Capital Transfers by the MDAs in subsidies, grants, or direct transfers to Semi-Autonomous Government Agencies (SAGAs) at Kshs.253.79 billion, representing 75 per cent of the gross development spending. Other major development expenditure comprised the Construction and Civil Works at Kshs.41.61 billion and the Purchase of Specialised Plant, Equipment and Machinery at Kshs.7.62 billion, representing 12 per cent and 2 per cent, respectively, of the gross development expenditure.
heading_path: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

blocks.text: A review of the recurrent expenditure shows that Kshs.469.97 billion was spent on Compensation to Employees excluding National Security Sector, and Semi-Autonomous Government Agencies/State Corporations, representing 39 per cent of the gross recurrent expenditure by MDAs and 27 per cent of the national government's equitable share of the revenue raised nationally and Appropriations- in- Aid. Th is was in line with the with the requirement of the PFM Regulations 26(1) of 2015 that the national government's expenditure should not exceed 35 per cent of the national government's equitable share of the revenue raised nationally plus other revenues generated by the national government under Article 209(4) of the Constitution. Total Current transfers to other government institutions were Kshs.507.12 billion and subsidies Kshs.68.26 billion, representing 42 per cent and 6 per cent of the gross recurrent expenditure, respectively. Other expenses with significant expenditure were Kshs.16.83 billion for travel, Kshs.9.79 billion for security operations, Kshs.8.20 billion for school examinations invigilation, and Kshs.6.87 billion for specialised suppliers.
heading_path: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

blocks.text: During the reporting period, budget implementation faced several challenges. Th ese included the accumulation of significant pending bills, which stood at Kshs.511.75 billion by March 2025, limiting cash flows and affecting suppliers' operations, especially SMEs. Low revenue outturn, with only 62 per cent of the annual target collected in the first nine months, occasioning delayed disbursement of funds and low absorption rates across MDAs and County Governments. Th ere was also irregular reliance on Article 223 of the Constitution to fund existing government programmes and settle predictable obligations, indicating weaknesses in the budget formulation process. Further, in-year changes to programme output targets undermined performance tracking, while delays in completing multi-year development projects further hindered effective budget execution.
heading_path: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

blocks.text: To address the challenges, the Controller of Budget recommends that the National Treasury fast-track the verification and settlement of pending bills and adopt more realistic revenue projections to reduce reliance on borrowing. Th ere is a need for improved fiscal planning and enhanced revenue collection, particularly from Appropriations-in-Aid. To strengthen expenditure management, government agencies should reduce reliance on Article 223 by ensuring better upfront budgeting for known expenditures. MDAs are encouraged to set specific and stable targets at the start of the financial year to facilitate accurate performance measurement. Lastly, priority should be given to completing ongoing multi-year projects before initiating new ones to enhance project completion rates and optimise resource utilisation.
heading_path: EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

blocks.text: 1.  INTRODUCTION
heading_path: 1.  INTRODUCTION

blocks.text: T his report is prepared in line with Article 228(6) of the Constitution of Kenya and Section 9 of the Controller of Budget Act, Cap 429, which states that, every four months, the Controller shall submit to each House of Parliament a report on the implementation of the budgets of the national and county governments. Section 9 of the Controller of Budget Act outlines the information to be contained in the report and states that, despite the first quarterly report, each subsequent report shall contain cumulative amounts from the beginning of that year.
heading_path: 1.  INTRODUCTION

blocks.text: Th e report is presented in six chapters. Chapter one is the introduction. Chapter Two presents the performance of receipts into the consolidated fund and exchequer issues released to MDAs, CFS, and equitable shareable revenue to the forty-seven counties by the National Treasury in the period under review.
heading_path: 1.  INTRODUCTION

blocks.text: Chapter Th ree is presented in four subsections. Th is includes the overall budget performance of the national government, performance under the Consolidated Fund Services (CFS), MDAs' expenditure by economic classification and the status of pending bills as of 31 st March 2025. Th e CFS comprises the public debt disaggregated into external and domestic, pensions and gratuities, salaries, allowances to constitutional office holders and miscellaneous services.
heading_path: 1.  INTRODUCTION

blocks.text: Chapter Four presents the budget performance of the eighty-one MDAs grouped into ten Sectors. Th e  ten sectors include (i) Agriculture, Rural and Urban Development (ARUD), (ii) Education, (iii) Energy, Infrastructure, and Information Communications Technology, (iv) Environment Protection, Water and Natural Resources, (v) General Economic and Commercial Affairs, (vi) Governance, Justice, Law and Order, (vii) Health, (viii) National Security, (ix) Public Administration and International Relations, (x) Social Protection, Culture, and Recreation sector. It presents the MDAs' performance on the approved budget, exchequer issues, actual expenditure, and project implementation status for some identified projects.
heading_path: 1.  INTRODUCTION

blocks.text: In the analysis of budget performance by MDAs, budget performance is reviewed at the gross and net estimate levels. Th e gross budget comprises Appropriations-in-Aid and government supply, representing the total vote allocation, while the net estimates represent the proportion of government supply to be funded through the exchequer. Th e budget data used in the report is based on the revised Supplementary Budget Estimates II approved by Parliament in March 2025, referred to as revised estimates. In examining the funding of planned activities by the government, exchequer issues are expressed as a percentage of the revised net estimates, while the overall budget expenditure is expressed as a percent age of the revised gross budget, referred to as absorption. On a linear basis, budget absorption is targeted to be 75 per cent of the annual budget as at the end of the first nine months of FY 2024/25 .
heading_path: 1.  INTRODUCTION

blocks.text: Chapter Five presents the key issues the Controller of Budget identified as hindering effective budget implementation and provides recommendations to address them. Chapter Six provides the conclusion.
heading_path: 1.  INTRODUCTION

blocks.text: Annexes support the chapters. Annex I presents major Foreign Currencies Movement, Annex II shows Capital transfer to SAGAs, Annex III details the MDAs' Recurrent Performance by Economic Classification, Annex IV shows Current Transfer, Annex V and VI show MDAs' and State Corporations/State Owned Enterprises/ SAGAs Pending Bills as of 30 September 2024 respectively, Annex VII presents the MDAs' Development Expenditure; Annex VIII details the Recurrent Expenditure, Annex IX, X and XI shows ministerial development and recurrent expenditure per sector and total expenditure per sector respectively.

blocks.text: 2. ANALYSIS OF RECEIPTS AND EXCHEQUER ISSUES
heading_path: 2. ANALYSIS OF RECEIPTS AND EXCHEQUER ISSUES

blocks.text: 2.1.  Introduction
heading_path: 2.1.  Introduction

blocks.text: Th is chapter presents the receipts into the Consolidated Fund and funds released by the National Treasury in the first nine months of FY 2024/2025. Th e funds released went towards funding Consolidated Fund Services, ministerial development expenditure, recurrent expenditure, and transfers to the forty-seven counties.
heading_path: 2.1.  Introduction

blocks.text: 2.2.  Revenue Estimates and Receipts into the Consolidated Fund
heading_path: 2.2.  Revenue Estimates and Receipts into the Consolidated Fund

blocks.text: Th e Consolidated Fund is established under Article 206(1) of the Constitution of Kenya and refers to the account into which all money raised or received by or on behalf of the national government is paid. It excludes monies reasonably exempted by an Act of Parliament and payable into other public funds established for a specific purpose or is retained by the State organ that received it to defray its expenses. Notably, at the beginning of FY 2023/24, the government directed that all money collected by all National Government entities as a fee on services offered be deposited into the e-citizen account, Pay bill number 222222.
heading_path: 2.2.  Revenue Estimates and Receipts into the Consolidated Fund

blocks.text: To finance the budget, the government, through the National Treasury, targeted to raise funds from various revenue sources. Th e sources include Tax Revenue (Kshs.2.40 trillion), Non-Tax Revenue (Kshs.180.20 billion), Domestic borrowing (Kshs.1.17 trillion - comprising of net domestic borrowing of Kshs.597.15 billion and internal debt redemption/roll-over of Kshs.569.89 billion), External Loans and Grants (Kshs.718.40 billion) and other Domestic financing (Kshs.8.52 billion). Th e Government also targeted to raise Kshs.573.52 billion from Appropriations in Aid (A-I-A) comprising Kshs.317.79 billion recurrent A-I-A and Kshs.261.16 billion development A-I-A.
heading_path: 2.2.  Revenue Estimates and Receipts into the Consolidated Fund

heading_path: 2.2.1  Receipts into the Consolidated Fund

Th e receipts comprised opening balances from the previous financial year (FY 2023/2024), Tax and Non-Tax Revenue, Domestic borrowing, External Loans and Grants, and Other Domestic Financing. blocks.text: 2.5.4  Approval for Withdrawals from the Equalization Fund
heading_path: 2.5.4  Approval for Withdrawals from the Equalization Fund

blocks.text: Th e Equalisation Fund is established under Article 204 (1) of the Constitution of Kenya, which requires that half a per cent (0.5 per cent) of all the revenue collected by the National government each year, calculated based on the most recent audited revenue received, as approved by the National Assembly, to be paid into the Fund. Article 204(2) of the Constitution provides that the National Government shall use the Equalisation Fund to provide only essential services, including Water, Roads, Health Facilities, and Electricity, to marginalised areas to the extent necessary to bring the quality of those services in those areas to the level generally enjoyed by the rest of the nation, so far as is possible.
heading_path: 2.5.4  Approval for Withdrawals from the Equalization Fund

blocks.text: During the first nine months of FY 2024/2025, the Controller of Budget authorised 20 requests amounting to Kshs.2.21 billion from the Equalization Fund. Th e amount comprises Kshs.198.50 million for the Equalization Fund Secretariat's recurrent expenses, Kshs.356.87 million for Policy 1 development pending bills under the Ministry of Water and Sanitation, and Kshs.1.66 billion for 2 nd policy development projects for 35 marginalised areas.

heading_path: 3. OVERALL BUDGET PERFORMANCE

blocks.text: 3.1.  Introduction
heading_path: 3.1.  Introduction

blocks.text: Th is chapter presents an overview of the National Government budget implementation in the first nine months of FY 2024/25. It also presents the budget performance of the Consolidated Fund Services (which is classified as recurrent expenditure), which contains information on Public debt, Pensions and gratuities, Salaries and Allowances to Constitutional officeholders and Miscellaneous services. Th e chapter further disaggregates expenditure for MDAs under major economic items for the development and recurrent votes, respectively. Th e recurrent vote comprises ministerial allocation and CFS votes. In addition, it presents the status of pending bills as of 31 st March 2025.
heading_path: 3.1.  Introduction

blocks.text: 3.2.  FY 2024/2025 Overall Budget
heading_path: 3.2.  FY 2024/2025 Overall Budget

blocks.text: Th e approved gross budget for the FY 2024/2025 amounted to Kshs.4.49 trillion, revised to Kshs.4.37 trillion in Supplementary Estimates I and Kshs.4.64 trillion in Supplementary Estimates II, presenting 2 per cent growth compared to Kshs.4.54 trillion in FY 2023/2024. Th is comprised of Kshs.616.09 billion for ministerial development expenditure, Kshs.1.73 trillion for ministerial recurrent expenditures, Kshs.2.29 trillion for CFS. Th is is a decline compared to Kshs.783.22 billion for ministerial development allocated in the FY 2023/2024. However, ministerial recurrent and CFS allocations increased compared to Kshs. 1.68 trillion and Kshs.2.08 trillion respectively allocated in FY 2023/2024.
heading_path: 3.2.  FY 2024/2025 Overall Budget

blocks.text: Th e government targeted to finance the budget through raising revenue of Kshs.2.75 trillion (including Appropriations-in-Aid) and a deficit financing of Kshs.1.89 trillion (to be funded by Domestic Borrowing, External Loans and Grants at Kshs.1.17 trillion and Kshs.718.40 billion, respectively). Th e Domestic Borrowing of Kshs.1.17 trillion is comprised of Net Domestic Borrowing of Kshs.597.15 billion and Internal Debt Redemptions of Kshs.569.89 billion. blocks.text: 3.3.2  Overdra ft Facility
heading_path: 3.3.2  Overdra ft Facility

blocks.text: Th e overdra ft facility is a way of short-term borrowing by the Government to cover temporary cash shortfalls. It is repayable within twelve months. Kenya's Government overdra ft is administered through the Central Bank of Kenya (CBK). It is restricted to a maximum of five per cent of the most recently audited revenues and is expected to be paid off by the end of the financial year as specified in Section 15 (3) of the PFM Act.
heading_path: 3.3.2  Overdra ft Facility

blocks.text: In the period under review, the overdra ft limit stood at Kshs.97.05 billion and was charged at an average interest rate of 12 per cent per annum on the amount outstanding at the end of each month. In the first nine months of FY 2024/2025, the total charge on the overdra ft facility was Kshs.5.2 billion, as shown in Table 3.5.

blocks.text: 4. BUDGET PERFORMANCE BY SECTOR
heading_path: 4. BUDGET PERFORMANCE BY SECTOR

blocks.text: 4.1.   Introduction
heading_path: 4.1.   Introduction

blocks.text: MDAs are classified into ten sectors according to the United Nations Classification of Functions of Government, designed to support fiscal analysis by breaking down Government Fiscal Statistics for comparability. Th e chapter presents the performance of MDAs by sector in the first three months of FY 2024/2025. It provides budget allocations per sector detailing specific MDAs' exchequer issues, expenditures, and absorption on the budget. Th e chapter also presents the performance of MDAs' programmes and sub-programmes and spending on development projects in the first three months of FY 2024/2025.
heading_path: 4.1.   Introduction

blocks.text: Sector performance is presented in alphabetical order as follows; (i) Agriculture, Rural and Urban Development (ARUD), (ii) Education, (iii) Energy, Infrastructure and Information Communications Technology (EIICT), (iv) Environment Protection, Water and Natural Resources (EWNR) (v) General Economic and Commercial Affairs (GECA) (vi) Governance, Justice, Law and Order (GJLO) (vii) Health (viii) National Security (ix) Public Administration and International Relations (PAIR) (x) Social Protection, Culture and Recreation (SPCR) Sectors.
heading_path: 4.1.   Introduction

blocks.text: In FY 2024/2025, the Education Sector was allocated Kshs.676.72 billion, recording the highest budget allocation, attributed to its broad mandate, including primary schools, secondary schools, special education, tertiary education, university education, examinations and curriculum development, and reforms in the education sector. Conversely, the General Economic and Commercial Affairs Sector received Kshs.60.77 billion, representing the lowest budgetary allocation.
heading_path: 4.1.   Introduction

blocks.text: 4.2.  Agriculture, Rural and Urban Development Sector
heading_path: 4.2.  Agriculture, Rural and Urban Development Sector

blocks.text: 4.2.1  Introduction
heading_path: 4.2.1  Introduction

blocks.text: Agriculture is a devolved function under the Fourth Schedule of the Constitution of Kenya. It is a critical sector in the economic pillar of the Kenya Vision 2030. Th e ARUD Sector comprises five sub-sectors, namely: Th e State Department for Lands and Physical Planning; the State Department for Livestock Development; the State Department for the Blue Economy and Fisheries; the State Department for Agriculture and the National Land Commission (NLC) together with affiliated Semi-Autonomous Government Agencies (SAGAs) and Training Institutions.
heading_path: 4.2.1  Introduction

blocks.text: Th e Sector is a significant player in the delivery of national development agendas, namely, Kenya Vision 2030, the government plan -the Bottom-Up Economic Transformation Agenda (2022-27), the Sustainable Development Goals, and the Agricultural Sector Transformation and Growth Strategy, among other national and international policies and obligations. During the MTEF period 2024/25-2026/27, the Sector has planned to implement programmes to facilitate food and nutrition security, agro-processing, employment creation, and utilisation of the blue economy.
heading_path: 4.2.1  Introduction

blocks.text: 4.2.2  Budget Performance for the ARUD Sector
heading_path: 4.2.2  Budget Performance for the ARUD Sector

blocks.text: Th e  budgetary allocation to ARUD in FY 2024/2025 amounted to Kshs.82.08 billion, which was revised to Kshs. 73.93 billion in Supplementary Budget I and Kshs. 80.47 billion in Supplementary Budget I I , compared to the Kshs. 98.09 billion allocated in the previous financial year of 2023/24. Th is amount represents 2 per cent
heading_path: 4.2.2  Budget Performance for the ARUD Sector

blocks.text: of the gross national budget of Kshs. 4.64 trillion and 3 per cent of the MDAs' budget of Kshs. 2. 35 trillion. Th e allocation included Kshs. 47.83 billion ( 59 per cent) for development activities and Kshs. 32.64 billion ( 41 per cent) for recurrent expenditure. Th e State Department for Agriculture received the highest budgetary allocation of Kshs. 45.64 billion (57 per cent of the Sector's budget), while the State Department f or the National Land C ommission had the lowest budgetary allocation of Kshs. 1.96 billion (2 per cent of the ARUD Sector allocation).
heading_path: 4.2.2  Budget Performance for the ARUD Sector

blocks.text: Th e high allocation to the State Department for Agriculture was due to its Vital role in Agricultural Policy and Research Management, National Food Policy, Strategic Food Reserves, Crop Development, Phytosanitary Services, International Compliance, Agricultural Farmers' Training, and Agricultural Land Resource Inventory management.
heading_path: 4.2.2  Budget Performance for the ARUD Sector

blocks.text: 4.3.  Education Sector
heading_path: 4.3.  Education Sector

blocks.text: 4.3.1  Introduction
heading_path: 4.3.1  Introduction

blocks.text: Th e  Education Sector comprises four MDAs: Th e  State  Department for Vocational and Technical Training, the State Department for Higher Education and Research, the State Department for Basic Education and the Teachers Service Commission (TSC) and their affiliated Agencies and Institutions.
heading_path: 4.3.1  Introduction

blocks.text: Th e Sector envisions attaining ' Quality and inclusive education, training and research for sustainable development '  in  Kenya. Th e  Sector's  strategic  objectives  include  enhancing access, equity, quality and relevance in education, training and research; establishing, maintaining and managing professional teaching and learning services for all early learning centres, primary, secondary and tertiary institutions; enhancing development capacities for Science Technology and Innovations; enhance mechanisms for dissemination and commercialisation of research findings; improve data quality and sharing in education, training, research and labour market; promote vibrant industry - institutional linkages in the area of skilling for employability; and integrate ICT in Education, Training and Research for management, teaching and learning at all levels.
heading_path: 4.3.1  Introduction

blocks.text: It is worth noting that the ongoing education transitions from the 8-4-4 to the 2-6-6-3 system require substantial infrastructure, equipment and human capital in FY 2024/25 and the medium-term 2024/25 to 2026/27.
heading_path: 4.3.1  Introduction

blocks.text: 4.3.2  Budget Performance for Education Sector
heading_path: 4.3.2  Budget Performance for Education Sector

blocks.text: Th e budgetary allocation to Education in FY 2024/2025 amounted to Kshs 656.55 billion, which was revised to Kshs.627.77 billion in Supplementary Budget I and Kshs.676.72 billion in Supplementary Budget II, compared to the Kshs. 689.40 billion allocated in FY 2023/2024. Th is amount represents 15 per cent of the revised gross national budget of Kshs.4.64 trillion and 29 per cent of the MDAs' budget of Kshs.2.35 trillion. Th e allocation included Kshs.26.53 billion (4 per cent) for development activities and Kshs.650.19 billion (96 per cent) for recurrent expenditure. Th e Teachers Service Commission received the highest budgetary allocation of Kshs. 366.25 billion 54 per cent of the Sector's budget), while the State Department for Vocational and Technical Training (TVET) had the lowest budgetary allocation of Kshs. 35.42 billion (5 per cent of the Education Sector allocation).
heading_path: 4.3.2  Budget Performance for Education Sector

blocks.text: Th e high allocation to the Teachers Service Commission is attributed to its vital role in the Teacher Resource Management programme. Figure 4.3 shows the budgetary allocation trends of the Education Sector from FY 2020/2021 to FY 2024/2025..

blocks.text: 4.3.18 Th e Teachers Service Commission
heading_path: 4.3.18 Th e Teachers Service Commission

blocks.text: Th e Teachers Service Commission is mandated to formulate policies to regulate the teaching profession and guide teacher management functions, thus ensuring compliance with the teaching standards prescribed from time to time, facilitating teachers' career progression and professional development and monitoring their conduct and performance during curriculum implementation.  TSC registers trained teachers and recruits, employs, and assigns teachers employed by the commission. It also exercises disciplinary controls over registered teachers, terminate the employment of the teachers, review the standards of education and training of persons entering the teaching service, reviews the demand for and supply of teachers, and advises the national government on matters relating to the teaching profession.

heading_path: 4.4.  Energy, Infrastructure and Information Communications Technology (EIICT) Sector

blocks.text: 4.4.1  Introduction
heading_path: 4.4.1  Introduction

blocks.text: Th is Sector consists of nine MDAs: Th e State Department for Roads, Transport, Shipping and Maritime Affairs, Housing and Urban Development, Public Works, Information Communications Technology and Digital Economy, Broadcasting and Telecommunications, Energy, and Petroleum.
heading_path: 4.4.1  Introduction

blocks.text: Th e EIICT sector aims to provide sustainable infrastructure development, a vibrant shipping and maritime industry, universal access to Information Communications Technology (ICT), Transport and built environment services, and accessible, affordable, quality and competitive energy and petroleum products.
heading_path: 4.4.1  Introduction

blocks.text: Th e EI&ICT Sector plays a vital role as an enabler of the country's socio-economic development. It is a crucial sector in realising Vision 2030 and the BETA Agenda.
heading_path: 4.4.1  Introduction

Th e allocation included Kshs.289.83 billion (66 per cent) for development activities and Kshs.147.75 billion (34 per cent) for recurrent expenditure. blocks.text: Th e State Department for Roads promotes the development of national roads development policy; develops, standardise and maintains roads; materials testing and advice on usage; protects road reserves; maintenance of security roads; administers mechanical and transport funds; registration of engineers; mechanical and transport services; and enforcement of axle load control. Th e mandate is carried out by the State Department for Roads and its agencies, Th e Kenya Roads Board, Kenya National Highway Authority (KeNHA), Kenya Urban Roads Authority (KURA), Kenya Rural Roads Authority (KeRRA), Engineering Board of Kenya and Kenya Engineering Technology Registration Board.

blocks.text: Th e State Department for Shipping and  Maritime Affairs promotes the maritime and shipping industry; manages maritime transport; ship registration; marine cargo insurance; human resource development, management and research in support of Kenya's shipping industry; establish an effective admiralty jurisdiction; develop a central data and information centre; co-ordinate maritime spatial planning and integrated coastal zone management; protect and regulate marine ecosystems; develop national capacity for Kenya's maritime sector; promote and facilitate placement of Kenyans in the global maritime labour market; protect the aquatic resources in EEZ; monitor and advising on usage of Kenya's exclusive economic zone; ocean governance and marine management; and government clearing and forwarding services. blocks.text: 4.5.  Environment Protection, Water, and Natural Resources Sector
heading_path: 4.5.  Environment Protection, Water, and Natural Resources Sector

blocks.text: 4.5.1  Introduction
heading_path: 4.5.1  Introduction

blocks.text: Th e Environment Protection, Water, and Natural Resources (EPWNR) Sector comprises six MDAs: State Departments for Environment & Climate Change; Forestry; Water and Sanitation; Irrigation; Wildlife; and Mining. Th e sector has several autonomous and semi-autonomous government agencies. In addition, it has the following entities: Th e National Environment Complaint Committee, the National Environment Tribunal, the Hydrologists Registration Board, and the Wildlife Clubs of Kenya.
heading_path: 4.5.1  Introduction

blocks.text: Th e goal of the Sector is to ensure sustainable development in a clean and secure environment with various objectives, including enhancing climate change resilience and low carbon emission, improving utilisation of land through irrigation and land reclamation, and promoting equitable and sustainable use of wildlife resources.
heading_path: 4.5.1  Introduction

blocks.text: Th e Sector plays a pivotal role in securing, stewarding, and sustaining the environment, Kenya's natural capital, water provision, and generating foreign exchange for the country. Th e Sector promotes socio-economic development to realise the Kenya Vision 2030 and BETA Agenda.
heading_path: 4.5.1  Introduction

blocks.text: 4.5.2  Budget Performance for EPWNR Sector
heading_path: 4.5.2  Budget Performance for EPWNR Sector

blocks.text: Th e budget allocation to the EPWNR Sector in FY 2024/2025 amounted to Kshs.109.73 billion, which was revised to Kshs.101.20 billion in Supplementary Budget I and Kshs.82.73 billion in Supplementary Budget II, compared to the Kshs.125.52 billion allocated in a similar period FY 2023/2024. Th is amount represents 2 per
heading_path: 4.5.2  Budget Performance for EPWNR Sector

blocks.text: cent of the revised gross national budget of Kshs.4.64 trillion and 4 per cent of the MDAs' budget of Kshs.2.35 trillion. Th e allocation comprises Kshs.48.69 billion (59 per cent) for development activities and Kshs.34.04 billion (41 per cent) for recurrent expenditure. Th e State Department for Water and Sanitation received the highest budgetary allocation of Kshs.30.15 billion (36 per cent of the Sector's budget), while the State Department for Mining had the lowest budgetary allocation of Kshs.1.59 million (2 per cent of the Sector's allocation).

blocks.text: 4.6.  General Economic and Commercial Affairs Sector
heading_path: 4.6.  General Economic and Commercial Affairs Sector

blocks.text: 4.6.1  Introduction
heading_path: 4.6.1  Introduction

blocks.text: Th e General Economic and Commercial Affairs (GECA) sector consists of eight MDAs, namely the State Departments for Trade; Arid and Semi-arid Lands (ASALs) and Regional Development; Cooperatives; Industry; Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises Development; Investment Promotion; East African Community; and Tourism together with their affiliated Agencies and Institutions.
heading_path: 4.6.1  Introduction

blocks.text: Th e main objectives of the Sector over the MTEF period are to transform Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs), promote and sustain tourism, promote industrial development investments, enhance trade and ease of doing business, promote growth and development of cooperatives and the MSMEs Sector, promote regional integration, and promote equitable and sustainable ASAL and regional development.
heading_path: 4.6.1  Introduction

blocks.text: 4.6.2  Budget Performance for GECA Sector
heading_path: 4.6.2  Budget Performance for GECA Sector

blocks.text: Th e  budgetary allocation to GECA in FY 2024/2025 amounted to Kshs.57.67 billion, which was revised to Kshs.45.63 billion in Supplementary Budget I and Kshs.60.77 billion in Supplementary Budget II, compared to the Kshs.78.67 billion allocated in the Financial Year of 2023/2024. Th is amount represents 1 per cent of the gross national budget of Kshs.4.64 trillion and 3 per cent of the MDAs' budget of Kshs.2.35 trillion. Th e allocation included Kshs.18.63 billion (31 per cent) for development activities and Kshs.42.14 billion (69 per cent) for recurrent expenditure. Th e State Department for Arid and Semi-arid Lands (ASALs) and Regional Development received the highest budgetary allocation of Kshs.15.07 billion (25 per cent of the Sector's budget), while the State Department for East African Community had the lowest budgetary allocation of Kshs.851.71 million (1 per cent of the GECA Sector allocation).

blocks.text: 4.6.3 Th e State Department for Trade
heading_path: 4.6.3 Th e State Department for Trade

blocks.text: Th e State Department for Trade promotes Trade Policy; Export Development and Promotion; Promote E-Commerce; Trade Negotiations and Advisory Services; Champion Trade Integration in the COMESA, CFTA, EPA, AFTA, etc.; Liaising and Coordinating with UNCTAD and WTO on Trade Matters; Enforcement of International Trade Laws, Negotiations and Agreements; Protection of Kenyan Goods against Dumping and Subsidised  Imports  and  recommending Countervailing Measures; Coordination of multi-Agency Task Force on the Elimination of Illicit Trade and Counterfeits; Liaison with International Trade bodies for National Development; Management of weight and measurement in Trade; Promotion and Regulation of the Wholesale and Retail Trade; and Promotion of Fair-Trade Practices and Consumer Protection. Th e mandate is carried out by the State Department for Trade and its agencies, the Kenya National Trading Corporation (KNTC), Kenya Export Promotion and Branding Agency (KEPROBA), Warehouse Receipt System Council (WRSC), Kenya Trade Remedies Agency (KETRA), Kenya Consumer Protection Advisory Committee (KECOPAC) and Kenya National Multi Commodities Exchange Limited (KOMEX).

blocks.text: Th e State Department for the ASALs and Regional Development promotes Arid and Semi-Arid Lands Policy; Coordination of Planning, and Development for Arid and Semi-Arid Lands; Implementation of Special Programmes for the Development of Arid and Semi-Arid Areas; Implementation of Arid and Semi-Arid Lands Programmes; Coordinating Research for sustainable Arid and Semi-Arid Lands Resource Management, Development and Livelihoods; Promotion of Livestock Development, Marketing and Value addition of Resources within Arid and Semi-Arid Areas; Enhancing Livelihood Resilience of Pastoral and Agro Pastoral Communities; Coordinating Responses Against Drought and Desertification; Special Programmes; Food Relief Management and Humanitarian Emergency Response; Peace Building and Conflict Management within Arid and Semi-Arid Area; Management and Promotion of Integrated Cross-border Activities in Identified ASAL Counties;  Regional  Development Policy Implementation, Oversight and Management; Coordination of Regional Development Authorities; and Projects in Response to Displacement Impacts. Th e mandate is carried out by the State Department for the ASAL's and Regional Development and its agencies, the National Drought Management Authority, Coast Development Authority, Lake Basin Development Authority, Ewaso Ngiro North Development Authority, Ewaso Ngiro South Development Authority, Tana River Development Authority and Kerio Valley Development Authority.

heading_path: 4.6.13 Th e State Department for Industry

blocks.text: Th e State Department for Industry promote and facilitates domestic and Foreign Investments; Investment policy and attraction; Industrial Policy and Planning; Buy Kenya - Build Kenya Policy and Strategy; promotes standardisation in Industry and Quality Control; Kenya Property Rights Policy (Patents, Trade Marks, Service Marks, and Innovation); Promotion of Value Addition and Agro Processing; Promotion, Development and Oversight of Aggregation and Industrial Parks; Textile Sector Development; Leather Sector Development and Promotion of Value Chain; Oversight and Regulation of the Scrap Metal Industry; Industrial Training and Capacity Development; To Combat Counterfeiting, Trade and Other Dealings in Counterfeit Goods; and Oversight, Administration and Enforcement of the Local Content Policy. blocks.text: 4.7.  Governance, Justice, Law and Order (GJLO) Sector
heading_path: 4.7.  Governance, Justice, Law and Order (GJLO) Sector

blocks.text: 4.7.1  Introduction
heading_path: 4.7.1  Introduction

blocks.text: Th e Governance, Justice, Law and Order (GJLO) Sector consists of sixteen MDAs, which include the State Department for Correctional Services; the State Department for Immigration and Citizen Services; the National Police Service; the State Department for Internal Security and National Administration; the State Law Office; the Judiciary; the Ethics and Anti-Corruption Commission (EACC); the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions (ODPP); the Office of the Registrar of Political Parties (ORPP); the Witness Protection Agency (WPA); the  Kenya  National  Commission  on  Human  Rights  (KNHCR);  the  Independent  Electoral  and  Boundaries Commission (IEBC); the Judicial Service Commission (JSC); the National Police Service Commission (NPSC); the National Gender and Equality Commission (NGEC); and the Independent Policing Oversight Authority (IPOA), as well as SAGAs and tribunals each with specific functions and mandates.
heading_path: 4.7.1  Introduction

blocks.text: Th e Sector creates a conducive environment for the country's economic, social, and political development necessary for fulfilling the objectives of the Kenya Vision 2030. It comprises institutions with linkages to peace- and security-building, interpretation of the law, correctional services, immigration and population management, legal advisory services to government agencies, representation of the national government in civil proceedings and matters before foreign courts and tribunals, and dispensation of justice. Further, the Sector promotes good governance and integrity and spearheads the fight against corruption, public prosecutions, registration and regulation of political parties, protection of witnesses, protection and promotion of human rights, delimitation of electoral boundaries and management of the electoral process, promotion of gender equality, the inclusion of marginalised groups and communities.
heading_path: 4.7.1  Introduction

blocks.text: Th e Sector is also responsible for developing and implementing citizenship and refugee management and immigration services, regulating the gaming industry, providing population management, eradicating drugs and substance abuse, conducting crime research, printing government documents, and overseeing policing.
heading_path: 4.7.1  Introduction

blocks.text: 4.7.2  Budget Performance for GJLO Sector
heading_path: 4.7.2  Budget Performance for GJLO Sector

blocks.text: Th e budgetary allocation to GJLO in FY 2024/2025 amounted to Kshs.246.42 billion, which was revised to Kshs.231.06 billion in Supplementary Budget I and Kshs. 255.73 billion in Supplementary Budget II, compared to the Kshs.252.49 billion allocated in the financial year of 2023/2024. Th is amount represents 6 per cent of the gross national budget of Kshs.4.64 trillion and 11 per cent of the MDAs' budget of Kshs.2.35 trillion. Th e allocation included Kshs.11.69 billion (5 per cent) for development activities and Kshs.244.03 billion (95 per cent) for recurrent expenditure. Th e State Department for National Police Service received the highest budgetary allocation of Kshs.115.43 billion (45 per cent of the Sector's budget), while the State Department for National Gender and Equality Commission had the lowest budgetary allocation of Kshs.437.70 million (less than 1 per cent of the GJLO Sector allocation).

blocks.text: 4.8.  Health Sector
heading_path: 4.8.  Health Sector

blocks.text: 4.8.1  Introduction
heading_path: 4.8.1  Introduction

blocks.text: Health is largely a devolved function under the Fourth Schedule of the Constitution of Kenya. Th e health sector is responsible for providing and coordinating health policy formulation, ensuring quality service delivery, and regulating health care at the national level. Th e sector comprises two MDAs: Th e State Department for Medical Services and the State Department for Public Health and Professional Standards. Th e Sector delivers services through several SAGAs and entities, including the Kenyatta National Hospital, Moi Teaching and Referral Hospital, Kenya Medical Research Institute, Kenya Medical Supplies Authority, Kenya Medical Training College, National Syndemic Disease Control Council, Kenyatta University Teaching, Referral and Research Hospital, National Cancer Institute of Kenya and the Kenya Nuclear Regulatory Authority.
heading_path: 4.8.1  Introduction

blocks.text: Th e Sector envisions 'a healthy, productive and globally competitive nation ' achieved through strategic objectives under equity, efficiency, and people-centred principles with a multi-sectoral approach as outlined in the Kenya Health Policy (2014-2030). Th e Health Sector implements its strategic objectives through eight budgetary programmes, four under the State Department for Medical Services and four under the State Department for Public Health and Professionals.
heading_path: 4.8.1  Introduction

blocks.text: 4.8.2  Budget Performance for Health Sector
heading_path: 4.8.2  Budget Performance for Health Sector

blocks.text: Th e  budgetary  allocation  to  Health  Sector  in  FY  2024/2025  amounted  to  Kshs.127.17  billion,  revised  to Kshs.118.86 billion in Supplementary Budget I and Kshs.136.08 in Supplementary Budget II, compared to the Kshs.138.85 billion allocated in FY 2023/2024. Th is amount represents 3 per cent of the gross national budget of Kshs.4.64 trillion and 6 per cent of the MDAs' budget of Kshs.2.35 trillion. Th e allocation included Kshs.32.01 billion (24 per cent) for development activities and Kshs.104.07 billion (76 per cent) for recurrent expenditure. Th e State Department for Medical Services received the highest budgetary allocation of Kshs.103.57 billion (76 per cent of the Sector's budget), while the State Department for Public Health and Professional Standards was allocated Kshs.32.51 billion (24 per cent of the Health Sector allocation).

blocks.text: 4.9.   National Security Sector
heading_path: 4.9.   National Security Sector

blocks.text: 4.9.1  Introduction
heading_path: 4.9.1  Introduction

blocks.text: Th e National Security sector comprise the Ministry of Defence and the National Intelligence Service (NIS). Th e sector's mandate is to ensure the country's security against any threats emanating from within or outside the Kenyan borders, defend the country, and support the civil powers in maintaining peace and order.
heading_path: 4.9.1  Introduction

blocks.text: 4.9.2  Budget Performance for National Security Sector
heading_path: 4.9.2  Budget Performance for National Security Sector

Th e allocation comprised Kshs.3.53 billion for development expenditure (2 per cent of the sector's budget) and Kshs.231.82 billion for recurrent expenditure (98 per cent of the sector's allocation). Th e Ministry of Defence was allocated Kshs.179.71 billion (76 per cent of the sector's allocation), while NIS received Kshs.55.65 billion (24 per cent of the sector's allocation). Th e growth in the budget allocation for the National Security sector is attributed to increased funding requirements for military modernisation, enhanced territorial defence capabilities, and strengthened intelligence-gathering operations.

blocks.text: 4.9.3 Th e Ministry of Defence
heading_path: 4.9.3 Th e Ministry of Defence

blocks.text: Th e Ministry of Defence encompasses the Kenya Army, Kenya Air Force, Kenya Navy, Defence Forces Constabulary and Civilian Staff. It envisions itself as a premier, credible, and mission-capable force grounded in professionalism. Its primary mandate is to defend and protect the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Republic of Kenya, while its secondary mandate includes assisting and cooperating with other authorities during emergencies or disasters and restoring peace in any part of Kenya affected by unrest or instability as directed. Th e Ministry is committed to defending and protecting the people and property of the Republic of Kenya against external threats and supporting civil authority as per the law.

blocks.text: 4.10.  Public Administration and International Relations Sector
heading_path: 4.10.  Public Administration and International Relations Sector

blocks.text: 4.10.1  Introduction
heading_path: 4.10.1  Introduction

blocks.text: Th e Public Administration and International Relations (PAIR) sector consists of twenty-three MDAs, namely Th e Executive Office of the President, Office of the Deputy President, Office of the Prime Cabinet Secretary, State  Department for Parliamentary Affairs, State Department for Performance and Delivery Management; State Department for Cabinet Affairs; State House; State Department for Devolution; State Department of Economic Planning; State Department for Foreign Affairs; State Department for Diaspora Affairs; Th e National Treasury; State Department for Public Service; Parliamentary Service Commission; National Assembly; Parliamentary Joint Services; Senate; Th e Commission on Revenue Allocation (CRA); Public Service Commission; Salaries and Remuneration Commission; Th e Auditor General; Th e Controller of Budget and Th e Commission on Administrative Justice (CAJ) together with affiliated SAGAs and entities.
heading_path: 4.10.1  Introduction

blocks.text: Th e  Sector  provides  national  leadership,  oversight,  and  policy  direction  towards  realising  the  country's  development agenda. It promotes prudent public finance management and accountability in the Public Sector, coordinates national and sectoral development planning, and oversees an efficient and effective Public Service. It also coordinates Kenya's foreign policy and diaspora affairs, wage bill management, development of a sound legislative and regulatory framework, and enforces administrative justice and the right to information.
heading_path: 4.10.1  Introduction

blocks.text: Th e  sector  has  prioritised  programmes  and  projects  aligned  with  the  Post-COVID-19  Economic  Recovery Stimulus Programme (PC-ERS), the Bottom-Up Economic Transformation Agenda, and the Fourth Medium Term Plan of Kenya Vision 2030. Priority was also accorded to ongoing interventions supporting the 'Big Four' agenda and the newly established institutions.
heading_path: 4.10.1  Introduction

blocks.text: 4.10.2  Budget Performance for the PAIR Sector
heading_path: 4.10.2  Budget Performance for the PAIR Sector

blocks.text: Th e  budgetary allocation to PAIR in FY 2024/2025 amounted to Kshs.331.20 billion, which was revised to Kshs.301.78 billion in Supplementary Budget I and Kshs.310.92 in Supplementary Budget II, compared to the Kshs.299.33 billion allocated in the previous financial year of 2023/2024. Th is amount represents 7 per cent of the gross national budget of Kshs. 4.64 trillion and 13 per cent of the MDAs' budget of Kshs.2.35 trillion. Th e allocation included Kshs.114.01 billion (37 per cent) for development activities and Kshs.196.90 billion (63 per cent) for recurrent expenditure. Th e National Treasury received the highest budgetary allocation of Kshs. 117.05 billion (38 per cent of the Sector's budget), while the State Department for Cabinet Affairs had the lowest budgetary allocation of Kshs. 0.22 billion (0.07 per cent of the PAIR Sector allocation).

blocks.text: 4.11.  Social Protection, Culture and Recreation Sector
heading_path: 4.11.  Social Protection, Culture and Recreation Sector

blocks.text: 4.11.1  Introduction
heading_path: 4.11.1  Introduction

blocks.text: Th e Social Protection, Culture, and Recreation (SPCR) Sector comprises six MDAs: the State Departments for Youth Affairs and the Arts, Sports, Culture and Heritage, Labour and Skills Development, Social Protection and Senior Citizen Affairs, and Gender and Affirmative Action.
heading_path: 4.11.1  Introduction

blocks.text: Th e strategic roles played by the Sector in the country's transformation and socio-economic development include Promoting and supporting youth empowerment and development; strengthening youth mainstreaming in  all  sectors;  spearheading  the  management  of  youth  policy  and  legislations;  promoting  engagement  with youth for national development; promotion of sustainable employment, harmonious industrial relations, and productive workforce; promotion of gender equity and equality; empowerment of communities and vulnerable groups, safeguarding children's rights; and advancement of diverse cultures, arts and sports to enhance cohesiveness and Kenya's regional and international competitiveness.
heading_path: 4.11.1  Introduction

blocks.text: 4.11.2  Budget Performance for SPCR Sector
heading_path: 4.11.2  Budget Performance for SPCR Sector

blocks.text: Th e budgetary allocation to SPCR in FY 2024/2025 amounted to Kshs.72.07 billion, revised to Kshs.68.94 billion in Supplementary Budget I and Kshs.70.21 in Supplementary Estimates II, compared to the Kshs.72.85 billion allocated in the previous financial year of 2023/2024. Th is amount represents 2 per cent of the revised gross national budget of Kshs. 4.64 trillion and 3 per cent of the MDAs' revised budget of Kshs.2.35 trillion. Th e allocation comprises Kshs.23.34 billion (33 per cent) for development activities and Kshs.46.87 billion (67 per cent) for recurrent expenditure. Th e State Department for Social Protection and Senior Citizen Affairs received the highest budgetary allocation of Kshs.35.33 billion (50 per cent of the Sector's budget), while the State Department for Culture and Heritage had the lowest budgetary allocation of Kshs.3.31 billion (5 per cent of the SPCR Sector allocation).
heading_path: 4.11.2  Budget Performance for SPCR Sector

blocks.text: Figure 4.18 shows the budgetary allocation trends of the SPCR Sector for the period FY 2020/2021 to FY 2024/2025.

blocks.text: Th e total exchequer issues to the SPCR Sector amounted to Kshs.40.85 billion, representing 84 per cent of the Sector's revised net estimates, comprising Kshs.3.66 billion for development expenditure, representing 58 per cent of development revised net estimates, and Kshs.37.19 billion for recurrent activities, representing 88 per cent of recurrent revised net estimates.
heading_path: 4.11.2  Budget Performance for SPCR Sector

blocks.text: In the first nine months of FY 2024/2025, the State Department for Social Protection and Senior Citizen Affairs received the highest proportion for both development and recurrent exchequer issues to revised net estimates at 91 per cent and 95 per cent, respectively. Th is is attributed to the release of funds towards the Safety Net Programme, which supports the vulnerable population. Th e State Department for Labour and Skills Development received the lowest proportion of development exchequer issues to revised net estimates at 9 per cent during the period under review.

Th is amount comprised Kshs.16.39 billion for the development budget representing an absorption rate of 70 per cent, compared to 56 per cent recorded in a similar period in FY 2023/2024, and Kshs.39.54 billion for recurrent expenditure representing 84 per cent of the revised recurrent gross estimates, compared to 67 per cent recorded in a similar period in FY 2023/2024. blocks.text: 5. KEY ISSUES AND RECOMMENDATIONS
heading_path: 5. KEY ISSUES AND RECOMMENDATIONS

blocks.text: During the reporting period, the Controller of Budget identified critical issues that impeded budget implementation. Th ese included the accumulation of huge pending bills, depressed revenue outturn, reliance on Article 223 of the Constitution to fund existing government programmes, in-year changes in programme output targets, and delayed completion of multi-year projects, as discussed below.
heading_path: 5. KEY ISSUES AND RECOMMENDATIONS

blocks.text: 5.1.  Accumulation of pending bills
heading_path: 5.1.  Accumulation of pending bills

blocks.text: Regulation 56 (1) (b) and (c) of the PFM (National Government Regulations, 2015 requires Accounting Officers to first factor in the budget contracts imposing financial obligations beyond one financial year to secure the resources required in line with the financing requirements set out in the contracts before new projects are budgeted.
heading_path: 5.1.  Accumulation of pending bills

blocks.text: Observation: Pending bills for the National Government MDAs amounted to Kshs.511.75 billion as of 31 st March 2025, representing 1 per cent decline compared to Kshs.516.27 billion reported as of 30 th June 2024. Th is comprised Kshs.421.63 billion (82 per cent) for State Corporations and Kshs.90.12 billion (18 per cent) for MDAs, compared to Kshs.379.82 billion and Kshs.136.45 billion, respectively, recorded in a similar period of FY 2023/24. Th e State Corporations' pending bills included unpaid obligations for development projects (62 per cent), consumables and general supplies (9 per cent), pension arrears (8 per cent) and unremitted statutory and other payroll deductions (6 per cent). On the other hand, MDAs' pending bills comprised of Kshs.67.13 billion for recurrent and Kshs.22.99 for development expenditure.
heading_path: 5.1.  Accumulation of pending bills

blocks.text: Accumulation of pending bills restrains cash flows to businesses, resulting in liquidity constraints, especially for Small and Medium-sized Enterprises, as they have to endure the long wait for settlement of overdue payments. Th is forces such businesses to either scale back operations, lay off workers, or even shut down operations. It also leads to high government costs of doing business due to the accumulation of interest charges and penalties on unpaid invoices, and it erodes trust between the government and the private sector.
heading_path: 5.1.  Accumulation of pending bills

blocks.text: Recommendation: Th e National Treasury should fast-track the verification of all pending bills of the National Government and implement the pending bills verification report, including hastened settlement of all bills assessed and cleared for payment.
heading_path: 5.1.  Accumulation of pending bills

blocks.text: 5.2.  Depressed revenue outturn
heading_path: 5.2.  Depressed revenue outturn

blocks.text: Paragraph 32 (10) of the Public Finance Management (National Government) Regulations 2015 provides that following the approval of the Budget Policy Statement, the national government entities or agencies shall finalize their estimates for years (N+1), (N+2) and (N+3) by 31st  March of the Financial year (N) and submit them to the Cabinet Secretary. Further, Paragraph 34 (a) requires the budget ceiling in the Budget Policy Statement to consider the aggregate resource envelope following the forecast of major revenue and expenditure categories.
heading_path: 5.2.  Depressed revenue outturn

blocks.text: Observation: Th e national government targeted to receive Kshs.4.47 trillion into the Consolidated Fund to finance the budget in FY 2024/25 as per the revised revenue projections. Th e targeted sources comprised Tax Revenue (Kshs.2.40 trillion), Non-Tax Revenue (Kshs.180.20 billion), Domestic borrowing (Kshs.1.17 trillion), External Loans and Grants (Kshs.718.40 billion) and other Domestic financing (Kshs.8.52 billion). In the first nine months of FY 2024/2025, receipts into the Consolidated Fund amounted to Kshs.2.75 trillion, representing 62 per cent of the revised annual target, which was below the 75 per cent target for the period when prorated quarterly. Th e receipts included opening balances from FY 2023/2024 (Kshs.1.16 billion), Tax Revenue
heading_path: 5.2.  Depressed revenue outturn

blocks.text: (Kshs.1.58 trillion), Non-Tax Revenue (Kshs.122.30 billion), Domestic borrowing (Kshs.731.60 billion), External Loans and Grants (Kshs.314.08 billion), and Other Domestic Financing (Kshs.4.44 billion).
heading_path: 5.2.  Depressed revenue outturn

blocks.text: Th e  underperformance in revenues led to constrained government cash flows, contributing significantly to the delays in releasing funds to MDAs and County Governments. Consequently, the CFS and MDAs recorded below-average budget performance during the period under review. Th e Ministerial development was the most affected, receiving 49 per cent of exchequer issues to revised net estimates and recording an absorption rate of 55 per cent. CFS received and recorded the second lowest exchequer issues to revised net estimates and proportion of actual expenditure in revised estimates at 53 and 58 per cent, respectively. County Governments received 61 per cent of the expected Counties' equitable share of revenues raised nationally. On the other hand, Ministerial recurrent expenditure, which received 70 per cent of exchequer issues to net estimates, recorded an absorption rate of 69 per cent.
heading_path: 5.2.  Depressed revenue outturn

blocks.text: Recommendation: Th e National Treasury should re-examine the government's fiscal planning by ensuring realistic revenue projections, avoiding ambitious budgets that may exacerbate borrowing. Th e Government should streamline revenue collections by expanding the tax base and sealing revenue leakages. Deliberate initiatives to improve collections from Appropriations-in-Aid by Ministries, Departments and Agencies, and County Governments may also reduce overreliance on funding from the Consolidated Fund.
heading_path: 5.2.  Depressed revenue outturn

blocks.text: 5.3.  Reliance on Article 223 of the Constitution to fund the Government's existing Programmes
heading_path: 5.3.  Reliance on Article 223 of the Constitution to fund the Government's existing Programmes

blocks.text: Article 223 of the Constitution stipulates the requirements for a supplementary appropriation. Paragraph 40 (3) of the Public Finance Management (National Government) Regulations, 2015 outlines the purpose for which approval can be sought for a supplementary budget. Th ese include (a) unforeseen and unavoidable circumstances where no budget provision was made or (b) unavoidable circumstances where there is an existing budgetary provision which, however, is inadequate . Further, Paragraph 40 (4) (a) of the said Regulations clarifies that expenditure that, although known when  fi nalizing the original budget estimates, could not be accommodated within allocations shall not be considered an unforeseen and unavoidable expenditure.
heading_path: 5.3.  Reliance on Article 223 of the Constitution to fund the Government's existing Programmes

blocks.text: Observation: During the first nine months of FY 2024/2025, the Cabinet Secretary (CS) of the National Treasury granted total approvals of Kshs.48.89 billion for additional funding to MDAS under Article 223 of the Constitution. From these approvals, the Controller of Budget authorized withdrawals of Kshs.42.22 billion from the Consolidated Fund. Scrutiny of the approvals revealed several instances where the reason for additional funding was to support existing government programmes and payment of pending bills, which should have been anticipat able during the budget formulation. For example, the State Department for Roads received additional funding of Kshs.8 billion from the Consolidated Fund and Kshs.4 billion from the Roads Annuity Fund under Article 223 in December 2024, mainly to settle outstanding pending bills. State House also benefited from additional funding that amounted to Kshs.1.16 billion under Article 223 of the Constitution to cater for utilities, rent, local visits, hospitality services, fuel expenses and maintenance of motor vehicles. Th e State Department for Social Protection and Senior Citizen Affairs accessed Kshs.1.24 billion in a separate instance as additional funding under Article 223, which was loan revenue that the World Bank had already disbursed into a designated project account to cater for the Kenya Social and Economic Inclusion Project (KSEIP), an ongoing project.
heading_path: 5.3.  Reliance on Article 223 of the Constitution to fund the Government's existing Programmes

blocks.text: Reliance on supplementary budgets to implement existing Government programmes or initiatives breaches Paragraph 40 (4) of the Public Finance Management (National Government) Regulations, 2015 and suggests
heading_path: 5.3.  Reliance on Article 223 of the Constitution to fund the Government's existing Programmes

blocks.text: potential lapses in the budget formulation process and/ or weaknesses in the budgeting cycle.
heading_path: 5.3.  Reliance on Article 223 of the Constitution to fund the Government's existing Programmes

blocks.text: Recommendation: Th e Controller of Budget recommends adopting good planning and budget practices and sound expenditure management by prioritizing all essential services and aligning them to operational realities.
heading_path: 5.3.  Reliance on Article 223 of the Constitution to fund the Government's existing Programmes

blocks.text: 5.4.   In-year changes in targets for programme outputs
heading_path: 5.4.   In-year changes in targets for programme outputs

blocks.text: Budget execution entails delivering services by undertaking expenditures within regulatory controls of the law by line Ministries, spending Departments, and Agencies. Controls in budget execution include mechanisms for monitoring actual expenditures and service levels by assessing how they align with actual financial outcomes and planned objectives throughout the implementation period.
heading_path: 5.4.   In-year changes in targets for programme outputs

blocks.text: Observation: Analysis of non-financial performance revealed in-year changes in the MDAs' output targets approved in the original budget of FY 2024/25. For instance, the State Department for Roads targeted the construction of 945 kilometres of roads in the approved original estimates, which was changed to 717 kilometres of roads as of 31 st March 2025. Also, review of the higher education support services programme implemented by the State Department of Higher Education and Research showed that targets for number of GOK students sponsored in public universities (260,450 students), number of GOK students sponsored in private universities (35,800 students), placement in universities (7,100 students) and research projects supported (50 researches) in the original budget were revised to  535,450 students, 67,600 students, 10,000 students and 35 research projects respectively, in the period under review. Further, the State Department for Lands and Physical Planning also revised its key output targets for the land policy and planning programme. Th e affected outputs included the number of title deeds issued (280,000), the number of landless/quarters settled (8,000) and the number of land parcels geo-referenced (50,000) appearing in the printed estimates, which were revised to 405,000 title deeds, 12,120 quarters settled and 75,000 land parcels geo-referenced respectively for the period under review.
heading_path: 5.4.   In-year changes in targets for programme outputs

blocks.text: Variation of annual targets over a financial year suggests moving targets, which poses a challenge in performance tracking due to the incomparability of performance at different time intervals in a given year.
heading_path: 5.4.   In-year changes in targets for programme outputs

blocks.text: Recommendation: MDAs are advised to set specific, realistic, and achievable goals to assess their activities at the commencement of a financial year. Th is ensures continuous improvement and alignment of efforts towards strategic objectives. Th ese goals should be the basis for stable targets that provide consistent and predictable measurements of progress.
heading_path: 5.4.   In-year changes in targets for programme outputs

blocks.text: 5.5.   Delays in completion of multi-year projects
heading_path: 5.5.   Delays in completion of multi-year projects

blocks.text: Observation: Reviews of MDAs projects' performance indicated general delays in project implementation, which affected the projects' completion rates. For example, the implementation of two projects by the state Department for Roads that began in April 2024 and had a target completion date of April 2025, namely; Mlango-Benon-State Lodge-Sach 3 - Riwo Pri - Store - Mto Mbili Road (10 per cent complete) and Chobe - Kambi George- Weru - Matundura & Muti-ini Th indi road (13 per cent complete), overstretched their planned completion dates. Besides, the construction of junior secondary classrooms and integrated resource centres across the country (21 per cent complete) by the State Department for Basic Education commenced in July 2021 and has a target completion date of 30 th June 2026. Further, four (4) development projects implemented by the State Department for Transport overshot their completion dates. Th e  projects  included  Development  of  Nairobi Railway City (completion date of 30 th June 2023), Construction of 2.8Km new MGR link from Mombasa SGR Terminus - Miritini S GR station and railway bridge across Makupa causeway (completion date of 30 th June
heading_path: 5.5.   Delays in completion of multi-year projects

blocks.text: 2024), Revitalization of Gilgil - Nyahururu MGR Branch line (completion date of 30 th June 2024), Construction of Access Road to Suswa SGR Station and to Maai Mahiu SGR Station (completion date of 30 th June 2024).
heading_path: 5.5.   Delays in completion of multi-year projects

blocks.text: Recommendation: MDAs should prioritize the implementation of ongoing projects by freezing the commencement of new projects and taking necessary measures to address project challenges, with a view to fast-tracking the completion of all the affected multi-year projects.
heading_path: 5.5.   Delays in completion of multi-year projects

blocks.text: 6. CONCLUSION
heading_path: 6. CONCLUSION

blocks.text: Th is National Government Budget Implementation Review Report sought to provide financial and non-financial information on budget performance for the first nine months of FY 2024/25 , covering 1 July 2024 to 31 st March 2025. It presents revenue outturn, debt financing, expenditure performance, and budget absorption and discusses key issues affecting overall budget execution.
heading_path: 6. CONCLUSION

blocks.text: During the period, the national government budget performance remained resilient despite the interruptions at the start of the financial year following the withdrawal of Finance Bill 2024, which affected revenue generation and budget implementation. Th e overall budget absorption rate was 62 per cent of the revised gross budget, which wa s below the target of 75 per cent in the first nine months of FY 2024/25.
heading_path: 6. CONCLUSION

blocks.text: Total receipts into the Consolidated Fund were Kshs.2.75 trillion, representing 62 per cent of the revised annual target. Th e Controller of Budget approved the withdrawal of Kshs. 2.64 trillion from the Consolidated Fund, representing 59 per cent of the revised net estimates, implying 16 per cent of targeted activities were not funded based on the target of 75 per cent in the first nine months. Th e exchequer issues comprised Kshs. 170.83 billion for ministerial development expenditure, Kshs. 991.75 billion for ministerial recurrent expenditure, Kshs. 122 tr illion for Consolidated Fund Services and Kshs. 255.54 billion as disbursements of equita ble share of revenues raised nationally to County Governments.
heading_path: 6. CONCLUSION

blocks.text: Gross expenditure for the National Government was Kshs. 2.86 trillion, recording an absorption rate of 62 per cent. Th is  comprised ministerial development expenditure at Kshs.338.18 billion (absorption rate of 55 per cent), ministerial recurrent expenditure at Kshs.1.20 trillion (absorption rate of 70 per cent), and Consolidated Fund Services at Kshs.1.31 trillion (absorption rate of 57 per cent). Th e development budget recorded the lowest absorption, implying delayed project implementation during the period under review.
heading_path: 6. CONCLUSION

blocks.text: Th e Controller of Budget identified key issues that hampered effective budget implementation and provided recommendations to remedy them in the remaining period of FY 2024/25 and the future. Th ese included the accumulation of huge pending bills, depressed revenue outturn , and irregular reliance on Article 223 of the Constitution to fund existing government programmes and predictable obligations. Other challenges included in-year revisions to programme output targets, which undermined performance tracking and delayed completion of multi-year development projects. Th e Controller of Budget recommends fast-tracking the verification and settlement of pending bills, adopting more realistic revenue projections to reduce reliance on borrowing, and improving fiscal planning and initiatives to enhance revenue collections from Appropriations-in-Aid. Other remedies include upfront budgeting for known expenditures, setting stable targets at the start of the financial year and prioritizing the completion of ongoing multi-year projects before initiating new projects.
heading_path: 6. CONCLUSION
